st.t: Automated evaluation: Stable scoring can preserve bad rubrics
st.an: JudgmentBench accepts the synthesis’s core distinction between scoring consistency and valid measurement of professional quality, then materially develops it through a paired attorney study showing that rubric scores can be weak summaries of constructed overall quality even when rubrics remain useful for criterion-level diagnosis and auditing.
qs: This asymmetry suggests a more nuanced reading of our results: rubrics are weaker as a summary of overall quality than the literature often implicitly assumes, but they remain valuable as an analytical instrument.

st.t: Legal benchmarks: Realistic tasks expose uneven competence
st.an: JudgmentBench accepts the need to evaluate realistic, open-ended legal work through expert assessment and materially extends the cluster by providing a public, paired comparison of rubric-based and preference judgments on the same professional work products. It also reinforces concerns about inconsistent and closed evaluation methods, though the supplied excerpts report no performance results and therefore do not independently establish uneven model competence.
qs: To our knowledge, it is the first publicly available expert-annotated legal benchmark in which the same outputs are evaluated under both rubric-based and comparative-judgment protocols, enabling direct comparison of the two methodologies on shared, high-judgment legal work products.
Its tasks were developed by formerly practicing BigLaw attorneys to reflect hypothetical, representative work products of the kind performed in litigation and transactional practice.

st.t: Legal quality: Scoring methods encode different harms
st.an: JudgmentBench accepts that legal-quality measurement depends on evaluation methodology and materially develops the cluster’s proposition by directly comparing rubric scoring with pairwise judgments. It reports better recovery of constructed quality differences, lower annotation time and stronger human–autograder ranking agreement, while limiting its claim to constructed work products and leaving causal explanations unresolved.
qs: The reliability of any benchmark, however, depends not only on the tasks it includes but on the methodology it uses to elicit and aggregate human or model judgments.
5   Discussion Our central finding is that comparative judgments recover constructed quality differences substantially better than rubrics, and do so in less than half the annotation time.

3.1    Base Dataset  The goal of our evaluation is to assess the application of quality metrics in law as a high stakes domain using a realistic set of tasks.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: JudgmentBench materially extends the cluster’s call for use-context-specific evaluation by empirically comparing two methods for assessing complex, open-ended legal work. It finds comparative judgment better recovers its constructed quality ordering and reduces annotation time, while preserving rubrics for explanation and auditing and limiting claims to the study’s design and context.

kp.k: Legal AI evaluation requires judgment beyond predefined answers
kp.d: The authors argue that complex commercial legal work is multidimensional and context-dependent, making output quality difficult to measure objectively. Case outcomes are inadequate proxies because facts, law, judicial preferences and strategy affect success independently of drafting quality. Their study compares rubric scoring with pairwise comparative judgment as methods for representing professional expertise in benchmarks.
qs: Defining “quality” in such a setting is particularly challenging as legal work products are frequently multidimensional, context-dependent and resist straightforward objective evaluation criteria
Strong briefs may fail due to adverse facts or judicial preferences, while weaker ones may prevail when the law clearly favors one side

kp.k: JudgmentBench releases expert assessments of commercial legal tasks
kp.d: The June 2026 paper releases 30 tasks drawn from Harvey’s proprietary 100-task BigLaw Bench: 16 transactional and 14 litigation tasks. The tasks represent hypothetical professional work rather than exam-style problems. The annotation dataset contains 1,539 rubric scores and 1,530 pairwise judgments over 2,274 unique outputs. Harvey provided tasks and associated data; Snorkel AI supported the project and supplied an annotator recruitment channel.
qs: Its tasks were developed by formerly practicing BigLaw attorneys to reflect hypothetical, representative work products of the kind performed in litigation and transactional practice.
In total, the sample comprises 16 transactional tasks and 14 litigation tasks.
Overall, the human annotation dataset contains 1,539 rubric scores and 1,530 pairwise preference judgments over 2,274 unique outputs for 30 tasks.

kp.k: Quality levels are constructed, not independently established ground truth
kp.d: Claude Opus 4.6 generated intermediate, good and excellent outputs by jointly varying analytical depth, precision, completeness, reasoning clarity, judgment and nuance. The researchers generated 50 variants per task–quality-level cell. A transactional attorney with over 30 years’ experience assessed realism; GPT-5.4 preferred excellent over good in 69 of 100 validation comparisons and good over intermediate in 67 of 100. The findings concern recovery of this prompt-induced ordering, not independently verified legal correctness.
qs: Ultimately, for each task, we constructed three work products using Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.6.
We induce quality variation by setting all 6 dimensions to either excellent, good or intermediate.
To reduce sensitivity to sampling variation from any single LLM generation, we generated N = 50 independent output variants for each task–quality-level cell.

kp.k: Experienced lawyers alternate evaluation protocols across tasks
kp.d: The study involved 51 annotators: six from an AmLaw 100 firm, five from AmLaw 200 firm Vorys and 40 recruited through Snorkel AI. Reported experience ranged from 3 to 35 years, with a median of 10. Although the paper describes paired signals from the same experts and items, its operational protocol assigned each lawyer only one methodology per task, alternating methodologies across successive completed tasks. Lawyers could skip tasks outside their expertise but not a methodology.
qs: Across all the experts, reported years of experience range from 3 to 35 years, with a median of 10.
Every successive task would then alternate between the two methodologies, such that annotators would do a task either under the rubric protocol or the comparative judgment protocol, but not both.
Annotators were allowed to skip tasks outside of their area of expertise, but were not able to skip a methodology.

kp.k: Comparative judgments better recover the constructed quality ordering
kp.d: Human comparative judgments achieved mean task-level Spearman correlation of 0.908 versus 0.150 for rubrics, a difference of 0.758 with 95% confidence interval [0.494, 1.021]. Pairwise win rates were 0.669 versus 0.542, a difference of 0.127 [0.067, 0.186]. Uncertainty was estimated using 2,000 hierarchical bootstrap iterations and normal-theory confidence intervals. The advantage persisted across task categories, experience and annotation-time subsets, and adjacent quality-level comparisons.
qs: Overall, our results indicate that comparative judgments have a consistent, material advantage over expert-developed rubrics in recovering our quality manipulation, both in terms of performance and time.
The advantage also holds for pairs of adjacent quality levels only (Appendix Table 5).

kp.k: Aggregated ranking recovery differs from individual judgment accuracy
kp.d: The rank-correlation metric measures pooled task-level rankings, whereas the win-rate metric measures individual comparisons, averaged across tasks. The authors caution that high pooled comparative-judgment recovery does not establish high individual accuracy: aggregation can recover the ordering when preferences favor higher-quality outputs in expectation and judgments are sufficiently independent. Additional rubric annotations instead converge on the rubric’s expected score profile, which may not match the intended construct.
qs: The rank-correlation estimand Dρ measures recovery of a pooled signal–the judgments of many annotators aggregated within each task-method combination–and is useful for benchmarking at scale.
First, a high R̄CJ does not necessarily mean that individual annotators identify quality well.
If the rubric’s criteria are only loosely correlated with the construct, no amount of additional annotation moves the pooled signal toward the truth.

kp.k: Preference assessment substantially reduces expert annotation time
kp.d: Median recorded annotation time was 1.92 minutes for comparative judgments versus 4.74 minutes for rubrics. Completed analyzed evaluations represented 242 hours and 15 minutes after excluding 56 records exceeding 30 minutes from timing calculations only. The approximately $242,000 figure is an equivalent billable-time estimate using $1,000 per hour, not reported expenditure: firm lawyers participated through pro bono programs, while Snorkel AI annotators followed its compensation policies.
qs: The advantage materializes despite comparative judgments requir- ing much less time than rubrics (median 4.74 minutes for rubrics, 1.92 minutes for comparative judgments).
Under the assumption of a $1,000 billing rate, the total billable hour equivalent of the annotations amounts to $242,000.
Annotators from law firms participated through the pro bono practices of their firms and did not receive additional compensation.

kp.k: Autograders show similar methodological advantages, not human equivalence
kp.d: GPT-5.4 also recovered constructed rankings better through comparative judgments: mean task-level rank correlation was 0.421 versus −0.250, while pairwise win rates were 0.599 versus 0.427. Human–GPT-5.4 ranking correlations were 0.375 for comparative judgments and 0.200 for rubrics. Corresponding human–GPT-5.4-mini correlations were 0.611 and 0.242. These results support the within-study protocol comparison without demonstrating that model graders reproduce expert judgment reliably in deployment.
qs: In particular, rankings following comparative judgments better recover our constructed quality rankings under both estimands, overall and within subsets of task categories (Appendix Tables 4a and 4b).
The mean task-level Spearman’s rank correlation between human and GPT-5.4 autograder-implied quality orderings is 0.200 for rubrics and 0.375 for comparative judgments.
for the smaller GPT-5.4-mini, with mean task-level Spearman’s rank correlations between human and autograder-implied quality orderings of 0.242 for rubrics and 0.611 for comparative judgments.

kp.k: Tacit expertise and cognitive load are proposed mechanisms
kp.d: The authors suggest two explanations for comparative judgment’s advantage: relative comparisons reduce cognitive demands, and holistic evaluation captures analytical depth, persuasive force and strategic judgment that predetermined criteria miss. Their design cannot determine which mechanism explains the results. They describe the advantage as more consistent among highly experienced attorneys but explicitly caution against overinterpreting that pattern.
qs: The first suggests that human raters discriminate more reliably between two stimuli than when assigning absolute values to one item in isolation; relative judgment imposes lower cognitive load and produces more stable signals across raters.
Our design cannot adjudicate fully between these mechanisms, but two patterns in the data are suggestive.
We are cautious about over-interpreting this gradient given our sample

kp.k: Rubrics retain diagnostic and auditing value
kp.d: The authors do not recommend abandoning rubrics. Preferences compress assessments into ordinal choices, while rubrics explain particular strengths and weaknesses and permit criterion-level auditing. They suggest comparative judgments as a possible default for legal evaluations, reserving rubrics for diagnostic needs, and propose hybrid approaches in which rubrics inform comparisons or are derived retrospectively from preferences.
qs: Annotations derived from comparative judgments collapse into a single ordinal preference, whereas rubrics can offer insights into why one output might be preferred over another.
Rubrics also support per-criterion auditing in ways that aggregated preferences cannot, which matters in deployment contexts where stakeholders need to understand what is being measured.
comparative judgments could be used as the default, with rubrics reserved for settings where the diagnostic information they provide is specifically required.

kp.k: Post-training implications remain an untested research agenda
kp.d: The paper connects evaluation design to the choice of reward signals for professional-domain model training. It reports prior studies favoring rubric-based supervision in other settings but questions whether those findings transfer to judgment-rich legal work with contested reference answers. JudgmentBench is intended to enable this comparison; the authors do not train models to establish which supervision method works better.
qs: We focus on evaluation in this paper; we do not attempt the training comparison, in order to keep the present contribution focused on the methodological question and the resource that supports it.

Whether the rubric advantage observed in more definitive domains carries over to high-judgment professional work is the natural next step, and one that the dataset’s paired structure is intended to support.

kp.k: Synthetic variation and limited overlap constrain conclusions
kp.d: All six quality dimensions moved together, unlike professional work that combines strengths and weaknesses; rubrics could perform better on such mixed cases. Stylistic markers may also allow preference judges to detect prompt conditions without evaluating substance. Different rubrics might improve rubric performance. Limited output overlap prevented a comprehensive inter-rater reliability comparison: repeated rubric assessments occurred 206 times, producing reported reliability of 0.442, while comparative-judgment pairs had no overlap.
qs: It is possible that rubrics compare more favorably against comparative judgment in such mixed cases, where their per-criterion decomposition can capture trade-offs that a holistic judgment collapses.
Second, prompt-induced variation may produce stylistic markers that correlate with quality level and that holistic judgment can detect even without engaging with substance.
Overlapping items were assessed by multiple annotators only 206 times for rubrics and not at all for comparative judgments, due to their pairwise structure.
Within rubrics, the IRR was 0.442, suggesting moderate agreement.

kp.k: Commercial US tasks limit professional and justice-system generalization
kp.d: The study is restricted to US commercial transactional and litigation work, excluding live activities such as depositions and negotiations and professional responsibilities such as mentorship and client development. The authors caution against assuming transfer to other legal systems. They separately recommend rigorous, client-centered evaluation research for legal aid and public defense; the study does not establish access-to-justice benefits.
qs: The tasks also do not cover dynamic legal tasks, such as taking a deposition or negotiating a live deal.
Both the underlying tasks and the annotators reflect the conventions of U.S. common-law practice.
In other settings such as legal aid and public defense, the development of legal AI tools around client needs demands a similarly rigorous approach to evaluation.

pts.k: Yang and coauthors claim that comparative judgment can make evaluation of AI-generated commercial legal work more informative and less time-consuming than rubric scoring; implications for model training remain prospective.
pts.d: The authors' central empirical claim concerns benchmarking and quality assessment, not replacement of lawyers or autonomous delivery of legal advice. Comparative judgments recovered their deliberately constructed quality ordering better than expert-developed rubrics and required less than half the annotation time. They suggest using comparative judgments as the default for legal evaluations while retaining rubrics when criterion-level diagnosis and auditing are needed. They propose that comparative judgment may capture tacit dimensions of legal expertise that predetermined criteria miss, but do not establish that mechanism. The dataset is also intended to support research into preference-based versus rubric-based model post-training; the paper does not test which produces better trained models.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims rest on an experiment using 30 tasks from Harvey's BigLaw Bench, synthetic outputs at three prompted quality levels, attorney annotations, and LLM autograder comparisons.
pts.d: The study includes 16 transactional and 14 litigation tasks, 51 annotators with a reported median of 10 years' experience, 1,539 rubric scores, and 1,530 pairwise preference judgments. Claude Opus 4.6 generated 50 variants per task and quality level. A lawyer with over 30 years of transactional experience reviewed the quality manipulation; GPT-5.4 provided additional pairwise validation. Human comparative judgments achieved mean task-level rank correlation of 0.908 versus 0.150 for rubrics, with a difference of 0.758 and reported 95% confidence interval [0.494, 1.021]. Per-judgment win rates were 0.669 versus 0.542, with a difference of 0.127 and interval [0.067, 0.186]. Reported median annotation times were 1.92 minutes for comparative judgments and 4.74 minutes for rubrics. GPT-5.4 and GPT-5.4-mini showed the same directional advantage. These statistics measure recovery of constructed quality differences, not legal accuracy against independently verifiable ground truth. The approximately $242,000 figure represents equivalent billable time at an assumed $1,000 hourly rate, not actual spending or demonstrated client savings. Although the abstract describes paired expert annotations, the detailed protocol specifies that an individual annotator evaluated each task under only one methodology.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The findings describe the June 2026 study setting; broader adoption and training implications have no specified forecast horizon and are explicitly conditional.
pts.d: The comparison applies to static, AI-generated work products representing U.S. commercial legal practice, evaluated with the particular rubrics and prompting procedure used. All six quality dimensions were moved together, unlike real work that may combine strengths and weaknesses. The authors acknowledge that comparative judgments might exploit stylistic markers and that different rubrics or mixed quality profiles could reduce their advantage. They do not claim generalization to non-U.S. practice, other specialties, live negotiation or depositions, or mentorship and supervisory work. High pooled rank correlation does not establish equally high individual judgment accuracy: aggregation depends on preferences favoring higher-quality outputs in expectation and on sufficient independence. Proposed explanations involving lower cognitive load and tacit expertise remain unconfirmed, and comparative judgment is not endorsed unconditionally over rubrics.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The direct implications concern legal-AI evaluation builders, expert attorney annotators, model developers, and stakeholders needing auditable assessments, principally in large-firm commercial practice.
pts.d: Benchmark designers and legal-AI developers could obtain a stronger overall quality signal with less expert annotation time in the tested setting. Attorneys supply the professional judgment being elicited; the authors cautiously suggest that comparative judgments may be especially useful for extracting senior practitioners' tacit knowledge. Stakeholders requiring explanations of particular strengths and defects retain a reason to use rubrics. The paper's released resource supports research into evaluation and potentially post-training, rather than demonstrating changes in law-firm staffing, billing models, client prices, or legal outcomes. Legal-aid and public-defense users are identified as important subjects for future evaluation research, not as populations shown to benefit by this experiment. Harvey is the legal-AI company providing the underlying tasks and associated data.
